title: Topology Stays Explainable
public_summary: A GraphReFly program should be understandable as named inputs, derived reductions, and boundary effects, not only as line-by-line control flow.

public_sections.heading: Guarantee
body: The graph shape is part of the public mental model. Developers should be able to inspect the declared nodes and edges that explain why an output changed.
bullets: Use the shared site for the cross-language graph shape.
Use package docs for exact factories and generated API reference.
Avoid hidden side channels that make work happen outside the declared topology.

public_sections.heading: Use It
body: Start by drawing the facts that can change, then place reductions and effects around those facts. When a composition grows, inspectability should improve the explanation instead of becoming an afterthought.

title: Async Stays at Boundaries
public_summary: External work can be asynchronous, but graph mutation re-enters through declared source, pool, or bridge boundaries.

public_sections.heading: Guarantee
body: Inside a graph, updates serialize through the graph's ordered update domain. File IO, network work, workers, remote graphs, and host callbacks belong at package-owned boundaries that re-enter with explicit graph facts.
bullets: Do async work in sources, pools, adapters, or bridges.
Keep ordinary reductions deterministic and inspectable.
Do not hide timers or callbacks inside the reactive core.

public_sections.heading: Use It
body: When you connect an external system, pick the package helper for that environment and let it publish explicit facts into the graph. The shared docs describe the boundary discipline; package docs own the runnable integration details.

title: One Graph, One Ordered Update Domain
public_summary: Within one graph, related updates settle in a single ordered domain so downstream reducers see a coherent input set.

public_sections.heading: Guarantee
body: A graph is the unit that keeps related propagation ordered. Parallel compute and remote graphs can exist, but their results return through explicit boundaries before they affect this graph.
bullets: Use one graph for one tightly related update domain.
Use pools for compute that must leave the immediate path.
Use bridges when separate graphs or runtimes need delayed consistency.

public_sections.heading: Use It
body: If two outputs must settle together, keep their shared cause inside one graph unless there is a real boundary. If there is a boundary, model it explicitly rather than pretending it is an in-process edge.

title: Missing Input Is Not a Fake Value
public_summary: GraphReFly keeps the difference between no value yet and a real domain value such as null, zero, or an empty collection.

public_sections.heading: Guarantee
body: A node should not compute from invented placeholder state. Missing input remains missing until a dependency produces real data, while domain-level empty values remain valid data when your domain allows them.
bullets: Do not bootstrap joins with fake objects or magic strings.
Let first execution wait for real inputs by default.
Use package helpers when you intentionally want partial-input behavior.

public_sections.heading: Use It
body: This guarantee keeps forms, loaders, retained views, and multi-input reductions honest. If a value is unknown, model that lifecycle directly instead of smuggling it through as ordinary data.

title: Joins Settle Predictably
public_summary: When one cause fans out and rejoins, the downstream reducer should see the settled result once, not a half-old mix.

public_sections.heading: Guarantee
body: GraphReFly coordinates fan-out and fan-in so a join waits for the changed inputs in the same update to settle before recomputing. That gives developers a stable way to reason about validation summaries, derived views, and other many-input reducers.
bullets: Declare every branch output the join depends on.
Let the graph coordinate the update order.
Do not manually trigger the join from each branch.

public_sections.heading: Use It
body: Model joins as reductions over declared dependencies. For a deeper walkthrough, use the composition guide; this page records the public guarantee.

title: Exact APIs Stay Package-Local
public_summary: The shared site teaches the common model; TypeScript, Python, and Rust own their generated API docs, runnable examples, demos, install notes, and release material.

public_sections.heading: Guarantee
body: GraphReFly has one shared developer-docs shell, but it does not hand-maintain mirrors of language package APIs. Each implementation package remains self-contained and owns its exact syntax and generated reference output.
bullets: Use shared pages for concepts, guarantees, and cross-language patterns.
Use language routes for package-specific APIs and examples.
Treat copied API mirrors in the shared site as a documentation bug.

public_sections.heading: Use It
body: When a public guarantee needs runnable code, follow the package links. The guarantee stays shared; the implementation details stay with the language package that owns them.

title: Languages Match by Behavior
public_summary: TypeScript, Python, and Rust do not need identical symbol lists to give developers the same core behavior where the protocol matters.

public_sections.heading: Guarantee
body: Cross-language consistency is checked through shared behavior scenarios. Language packages may expose idiomatic helpers, but the important question is whether the same graph situation settles the same way.
bullets: Expect package APIs to feel native to their language.
Expect core behavior to be checked by shared scenarios.
Do not use the shared site as a generated API comparison table.

public_sections.heading: Use It
body: Choose the package for your runtime, then rely on the shared guarantees for the common behavior. When you need exact syntax, follow that package's docs.
